doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Jazz education versus learning on the bandstand
summary: Both argue that too much theory can block the ear and that mentoring on the bandstand is the best way to learn and find your own voice.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I recently read a statement said by the fella that you happen to be playing with tonight, that he actually, in retrospect, feels more fortunate that there wasn’t all this jazz education available when he was learning. Do you have any feeling on that statement?

Well I understand what this fellow meant in that, and I see it happening myself through my own teaching, that you know it’s very easy for a young musician who is in the educational system and the process to become so absorbed with theoretical knowledge and the black and white on paper of this or that that they miss the real bottom line of the whole thing which is the ear and creating music. Hearing something to play. You know what I mean? It’s almost like a block that can happen with some of them, not always. But maybe some of those people who are almost overloaded by theoretical information, maybe some of those people could be further along in their playing if they had approached it in a less academic way.

More hands on. More hands on. I mean the best way to learn about this music is by doing it, and learning, for me, has been a constant evolution where only so much can come from books and come from things that you see. So much has to be done on the bandstand. The process of learning. Sitting next to musicians who are older and wiser, and basically getting humbled by people on the bandstand, where you basically get your ass kicked by people that play better than you and you learn through doing. And unfortunately, well unfortunately there’s less opportunities for that to occur because the big bands don’t exist so much, jazz is not the popular music of our time, where in the older days it was more popular, you always had the opportunity hands on through the whole mentoring reality, where you’d be with older musicians who were more knowledgeable and you’d learn by being next to them. And it’s like how did you learn how to walk? You didn’t read it out of a book. You saw somebody do it, and you tried to do it, you fell down, you got up, you did it again. And you learn through doing. And consequently because there are not these opportunities for young musicians as far as this mentoring opportunity, the educational system is taking up some of that slack, which is very good. But we can’t lose sight of the whole reality of trying to find a voice, trying to find your own thing, your own sound. It’s not like how well can I be a Xerox of somebody else, but how can I take all the elements that are out there, learn as much as I can through — imitation is part of the learning © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

process — but then how can I find out how I can be the best that I can be. I mean in the old days it used to be you’d listen to somebody and you could tell who they were right away, it’s like they sang their own song. Now a lot of musicians it’s like they’re singing somebody else’s song, and what’s their song. You know what I mean?
